text:
Former Delta State Governor Emmanuel Uduaghan has died at the age of 71, three days before his 72nd birthday.
Uduaghan died on Monday morning, October 19, 2026, according to a statement issued on behalf of the family by Toju Anire Uduaghan.
The family described his death as a profound loss, saying he was a source of strength and a father figure whose life touched many people in Delta State and beyond.
“His passing has left us devastated. Words can hardly express the depth of our sorrow at the loss of a man who meant so much to our family and whose life and service touched countless others across Delta State and Nigeria,” the statement said.
Born on October 22, 1954, Uduaghan was a medical doctor of Itsekiri origin from Warri North Local Government Area of Delta State.
He governed the state from 2007 to 2015, a period marked by political controversies, infrastructure projects, sporting achievements and a fierce struggle over his successor.
Before becoming governor, he served as Commissioner for Health from May 1999 to May 2003 under former Governor James Ibori.
He was later appointed Secretary to the State Government in June 2003, a position he held until the end of Ibori’s administration in 2007.
Uduaghan attended Federal Government College, Warri, from 1968 to 1974 and studied medicine at the University of Benin from 1975 to 1980, earning an MBBS degree. He also obtained a diploma in Anaesthesia.
Uduaghan’s eight years in office were marked by political battles, including controversies over his predecessor’s corruption allegations and a struggle to determine who would succeed him.
His first tenure was briefly interrupted when the Court of Appeal nullified his election shortly before the 2011 general elections.
The Speaker of the Delta State House of Assembly, Sam Obi, served as acting governor for about three months before Uduaghan won the rerun election and returned to office.
His administration also faced criticism over its handling of allegations against Ibori, who was eventually convicted of corruption-related offences in the United Kingdom and sentenced to prison.
Critics accused Uduaghan of failing to investigate and prosecute his predecessor despite allegations and petitions against him.
The controversy remained a significant part of the political narrative surrounding his administration.
Although some associates described Uduaghan as generous during his years as commissioner and secretary to the state government, others reportedly felt his approach to spending changed after he became governor.
Unlike Ibori, whose administration embarked on several ambitious projects, Uduaghan was not widely associated with a similarly expansive construction programme.
One explanation offered at the time was that his government faced financial obligations inherited from his predecessor.
However, his administration recorded notable infrastructure and sporting achievements.
Among its prominent projects were flyovers at Effurun in Warri and along Summit Road in Asaba. The Summit Road flyover was later named after him.
His government also sustained Delta State’s strong position in Nigerian sports. The state won the National Sports Festival in successive editions during his administration.
Uduaghan’s tenure was also associated with the rise of Delta-born football administrator Amaju Pinnick, who became president of the Nigeria Football Federation.
One of the biggest setbacks of Uduaghan’s political career was his failure to install his preferred successor in 2015.
He initially backed Tony Obuh, a permanent secretary from Ika, to succeed him.
He later dropped that position and supported David Edevbie, an Urhobo politician widely regarded as Ibori’s preferred candidate.
The succession battle exposed divisions within the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), which was then the ruling party in the state.
Amid the contest, Ifeanyi Okowa emerged as the party’s governorship candidate and won the general election, succeeding Uduaghan in May 2015.
Uduaghan’s attempt to move to the Senate in the same year also ended in defeat. He first sought the PDP ticket for Delta South but lost the nomination to the incumbent, Senator James Manager.
He subsequently defected to the All Progressives Congress (APC) and secured its senatorial ticket, but Manager defeated him again in the general election.
The twin defeats marked a major setback for his political ambitions.
After leaving office and losing the senatorial election, Uduaghan maintained a relatively low public profile as his involvement in active politics diminished.
His reduced public appearances in later years also coincided with concerns about his health, which fuelled rumours of his death on several occasions before his death was confirmed on Monday.
Meanwhile, the Delta State Government has declared three days of mourning in honour of Uduaghan.
Governor Sheriff Oborevwori directed that all flags on public buildings across the state be flown at half-mast throughout the three-day mourning period.
Oborevwori, in a condolence message by his spokesman, Festus Ahon, described Uduaghan as a detribalised leader whose contributions to the development of the state would not be forgotten.
The governor sympathised with the late former governor’s wife, Roli, his children, the entire Uduaghan family, the Itsekiri nation and Deltans over the painful loss.
He described the former governor as a leader who looked beyond ethnic differences and worked for the overall development of Delta State.
Oborevwori said Uduaghan’s years in public service had left a good mark on the state, adding that his death was a loss to Delta and the country at large.
